Find the area of the shaded sector using A = half r squared theta.

blocks.task_summary: Write down the equations of the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of f(x) = 1 - 1/(x - 2).
method_path: Vertical asymptote: denominator x - 2 = 0 gives x = 2
Horizontal asymptote: as x tends to plus/minus infinity, 1/(x - 2) tends to 0 so y = 1

evidence.basis: (a)(i) x = 2 A1; (a)(ii) y = 1 A1; [2 marks]

blocks.task_summary: Find the coordinates where the graph of f(x) = 1 - 1/(x - 2) intersects the y-axis and the x-axis.
method_path: x-intercept: set f(x) = 0, 1 - 1/(x - 2) = 0 gives 1/(x - 2) = 1 gives x - 2 = 1 gives x = 3 gives (3, 0)

blocks.task_summary: Sketch the graph of y = f(x) showing all asymptotes and intercepts found in parts (a) and (b).
method_path: Sketch two branches of hyperbola with vertical asymptote x = 2, horizontal asymptote y = 1, y-intercept (0, 3/2), and x-intercept (3, 0)

evidence.basis: (c) two correct branches with correct asymptotic behaviour and intercepts clearly shown A1; [1 mark] Total [5 marks]

blocks.task_summary: Find P(B) given P(A)=0.4, P(A|B)=0.25, and P(A∪B)=0.55 by combining the addition rule and conditional probability formula.
method_path: Express P(A∩B)=0.25P(B) and substitute into the first equation

evidence.basis: substitutes into P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B) to form 0.55=0.4+P(B)−P(A∩B) (or equivalent) (A1)
substitutes into P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) to form 0.25=P(A∩B)/P(B) (or equivalent) (A1)
attempts to combine their two probability equations to form an equation in P(B) (M1)
correct equation in P(B): 0.55=0.4+P(B)−0.25P(B) OR P(B)−0.15=0.25P(B) OR (P(B)−0.15)/0.25=P(B) (or equivalent) A1

blocks.task_summary: Set up definite integral for area under y=x/(x^2+2) from 0 to c, integrate by substitution or inspection to obtain (1/2)ln(x^2+2), substitute limits, equate to ln 3, apply log laws, then solve c^2=16 to give c=4.
method_path: Set up A = integral from 0 to c of x/(x^2+2) dx
Integrate by substitution u=x^2+2 to get (1/2)ln|u| or by inspection to get (1/2)ln(x^2+2)
accepted_alternatives: Integrate by substitution using u=x^2 (rather than u=x^2+2)
Apply log law to obtain ln((c^2+2)/2) = ln 3 with (c^2+2)/2 = 3 as intermediate step before reaching (c^2+2)/2 = 9

evidence.basis: Definite integral setup A = integral_0^c x/(x^2+2) dx; EITHER substitution u=x^2+2 or u=x^2 (M1); integrated form (1/2)[ln|u+2|] or (1/2)ln(x^2+2) (A1); OR integration by inspection (M1) yielding (1/2)ln(x^2+2) (A1)
THEN correctly substitutes limits (M1); correctly applies at least one log law (M1); obtains (c^2+2)/2 = 9 or (c^2+2)/2 = 3 (A1); then c^2=16, c=4 (A1). Total [6 marks].

blocks.task_summary: Form the composite (g∘f)(x) = (ax+b)² + (ax+b) + 3, expand, equate coefficients with 4x²−14x+15 to obtain a²=4 and 2ab+a=−14, solve for a=±2 then find corresponding b=−4 and b=3, giving f(x)=2x−4 and f(x)=−2x+3.
method_path: Expand to a²x² + 2abx + b² + ax + b + 3 and equate to 4x² − 14x + 15
For a = 2, solve 4b + 2 = −14 → b = −4, giving f(x) = 2x − 4
For a = −2, solve −4b − 2 = −14 → b = 3, giving f(x) = −2x + 3

evidence.basis: M1 for attempts to form (g∘f)(x); A1 for expanded form a²x²+2abx+b²+ax+b+3=4x²−14x+15; M1 for equating corresponding terms; A1 for a=±2; M1 for using 2ab+a=−14 to pair values; A1A1 for f(x)=2x−4 and f(x)=−2x+3.

blocks.task_summary: State E(X) for a continuous uniform distribution on [a, 3a].

evidence.basis: E(X) = 2a (by symmetry) A1

blocks.task_summary: Use integration to find Var(X) for a continuous uniform distribution on [a, 3a].
accepted_alternatives: Apply Var(X) = E[(X − E(X))²]: compute ∫_a^{3a} (x−2a)²/(2a) dx = [(x−2a)³/(6a)]_a^{3a} = a²/3

evidence.basis: METHOD 1: uses Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² (M1); integration expression A1; intermediate value (A1); final A1 for a²/3
METHOD 2: uses Var(X) = E[(X − E(X))²] (M1); integration A1; intermediate (A1); final A1 for a²/3

blocks.task_summary: Prove by mathematical induction that ∑_{r=1}^{n} r/((r+1)!) = 1 − 1/((n+1)!) for all integers n ≥ 1.
method_path: Verify base case n=1: LHS = 1/2, RHS = 1/2, so P(1) true
Conclude P(k+1) true, hence by induction P(n) true for all n ≥ 1

evidence.basis: R1 for verifying base case P(1) with LHS=1/2, RHS=1/2. M1 for assuming P(k) true. (M1) for writing P(k+1) sum as P(k) sum plus (k+1)/((k+2)!). A1 for substituting hypothesis to get 1−1/((k+1)!)+(k+1)/((k+2)!). A1 for intermediate simplification step. A1 for final form 1−1/((k+2)!). R1 for concluding P(k+1) true and hence P(n) true for all n≥1 (requires any four prior marks). Total 7 marks. Note: M1 not awarded for mere 'let n=k'.

blocks.task_summary: Show that cos^2 k = sin k, where k is the x-coordinate of the intersection point P of f(x) = cos x and g(x) = tan x.
method_path: Equate f(k) = g(k): cos k = tan k
Substitute tan k = sin k / cos k
Multiply both sides by cos k: cos^2 k = sin k

evidence.basis: sin k / cos k = cos k then cos^2 k = sin k AG

blocks.task_summary: Show that the tangent to y = f(x) at P and the tangent to y = g(x) at P intersect at right angles, using cos^2 k = sin k from part (a).
method_path: Differentiate f to obtain f'(k) = -sin k
Differentiate g to obtain g'(k) = sec^2 k
Compute product f'(k) g'(k) = -sin k sec^2 k = -sin k / cos^2 k
Substitute cos^2 k = sin k from part (a)
Conclude f'(k) g'(k) = -1, so tangents are perpendicular
accepted_alternatives: Show g'(k) = 1/cos^2 k = 1/sin k, then g'(k) = -1/f'(k), hence tangents are perpendicular.

evidence.basis: f'(k) = -sin k and g'(k) = sec^2 k A1
EITHER f'(k)g'(k) = -sin k/cos^2 k = -1 OR g'(k) = 1/cos^2 k = 1/sin k = -1/f'(k); R1 for conclusion that tangents intersect at right angles

blocks.task_summary: Find the value of sin k in the form (a + sqrt(b))/c, where a, c in Z and b in Z+.
method_path: Apply cos^2 k = 1 - sin^2 k with cos^2 k = sin k
Rearrange: 1 - sin^2 k = sin k to sin^2 k + sin k - 1 = 0
Apply quadratic formula: sin k = (-1 +/- sqrt(1+4))/2
Select positive root: sin k = (-1 + sqrt(5))/2

evidence.basis: 1 - sin^2 k = sin k (from part a) A1; attempts to solve for sin k (M1); sin k = (-1+sqrt(5))/2 A1; a=-1, b=5, c=2

blocks.task_summary: Express OM and MC in terms of a and c.
method_path: MC = OC − OM = c − (a + kc) = (1−k)c − a

evidence.basis: OM = a + kc (A1); MC = (1−k)c − a (A1)

blocks.task_summary: Use a vector method to show that |a|²(1−2k)(2cosθ−(1−2k))=0.

evidence.basis: M1: attempts to expand their dot product (a+kc)·((1−k)c−a); M1: uses |c|²=4|a|² and a·c=2|a|²cosθ; A1: correct result leading to AG

blocks.task_summary: Find the range of values for θ such that there are two possible positions for M.
method_path: Set each factor to zero from |a|²(1−2k)(2cosθ−(1−2k))=0 with |a|≠0
Exclude θ=π/2 (gives k=1/2, a unique M)
accepted_alternatives: Solve for cosθ instead of k: cosθ=(1−2k)/2, then apply 0≤k≤1 to obtain the same bounds on cosθ.

evidence.basis: M1: attempts to solve (1−2k)(2cosθ−(1−2k))=0 for k (or for cosθ); k=1/2 or k=(1−2cosθ)/2; A1: 0≤(1−2cosθ)/2≤1 → −1/2≤cosθ≤1/2; A1A1: π/3≤θ≤2π/3, θ≠π/2

blocks.task_summary: Show that for point Q on the circle x^2 + y^2 = 9 in the first quadrant, y = sqrt(9 - x^2).
method_path: Rearrange x^2 + y^2 = 9 to y^2 = 9 - x^2
Since Q is in first quadrant, y > 0 implies y = sqrt(9 - x^2)

evidence.basis: y = sqrt(9 - x^2) OR y = +/- sqrt(9 - x^2) A1, then since y > 0 yields y = sqrt(9 - x^2) AG. [1 mark]

blocks.task_summary: Find an expression for A, the area of triangle PQR, in terms of x.
accepted_alternatives: Equivalent forms such as (x + 3) sqrt(9 - x^2)

evidence.basis: b = 2y = 2 sqrt(9 - x^2) or h = x + 3 (A1). Attempts to substitute into A = (1/2)bh (M1). A = sqrt(9 - x^2)(x + 3) A1. [3 marks]

blocks.task_summary: Show that dA/dx = (9 - 3x - 2x^2) / sqrt(9 - x^2).
method_path: Apply product rule to A = sqrt(9 - x^2) * (x + 3)
Apply chain rule: d/dx[sqrt(9 - x^2)] = -x / sqrt(9 - x^2)
Combine terms and simplify to obtain (9 - 3x - 2x^2) / sqrt(9 - x^2)
accepted_alternatives: Method 2: Use dA/dx = (dA/dy)*(dy/dx) with A = y(x+3) and dy/dx = -x/y, substitute and simplify.

evidence.basis: METHOD 1: attempts product rule (M1), attempts chain rule (M1), two A1 for derivative simplification. METHOD 2: dA/dx = dA/dy * dy/dx with A = y(x+3) and dy/dx = -x/y. [4 marks]

blocks.task_summary: Find the y-coordinate of R such that area A is a maximum.
method_path: Solve quadratic: (2x - 3)(x + 3) = 0, giving x = 3/2 or x = -3
accepted_alternatives: Solve quadratic via formula: x = (3 +/- sqrt(9 - 4(-2)(9))) / (2(-2)) giving x = 3/2 or x = -3.

evidence.basis: Set dA/dx = 0 (M1). Attempts to solve 9 - 3x - 2x^2 = 0 (M1). (2x - 3)(x + 3) = 0 OR quadratic formula (A1). x = 3/2 A1. Substitute into y = -sqrt(9 - x^2) (M1). y = -sqrt(27/4) = -3 sqrt(3)/2 A1. [6 marks]

blocks.task_summary: Find modulus and argument of u = -1 + √3 i, hence show u = 2e^(2πi/3).
accepted_alternatives: METHOD 2: use polar form equations r cos(2π/3) = −1 and r sin(2π/3) = √3 to find r = 2, then combine with argument from diagram/tan to give 2e^(2πi/3).

evidence.basis: A1 for |u| = √((−1)²+(√3)²) = 2 (AG); M1 for reference angle π/3 or tan⁻¹(√3/1); A1 for arg = π − π/3 = 2π/3, giving 2e^(2πi/3) (AG). METHOD 2: M1 for reference angle; A1 for argument; A1 for r = 2 via cos(2π/3) or sin(2π/3).

blocks.task_summary: (i) Find smallest positive integer n such that u^n is real. (ii) Evaluate u^n for that n.
method_path: (i) Write u^n = 2^n e^(2nπi/3); for u^n ∈ ℝ require sin(2nπ/3) = 0
Set 2nπ/3 = kπ, k ∈ ℤ → n = 3k/2; smallest positive integer n = 3
accepted_alternatives: Any correct reasoning that n must be a multiple of 3 to make the argument an integer multiple of π, with n = 3 being the smallest positive such integer.

evidence.basis: (i) (M1) for noting u^n ∈ ℝ ⇒ 2nπ/3 = kπ; (A1) for a multiple of 3 considered; A1 for n = 3. (ii) M1 for substituting their n into u^n; A1 for u³ = 8.

blocks.task_summary: (i) Given u = −1+√3i is a root of z³+5z²+10z+12=0, find the other roots. (ii) Using a transformation or otherwise, find the roots of 1+5w+10w²+12w³=0.
method_path: (i) By conjugate root theorem, −1−√3i is a root
accepted_alternatives: (i) OR: form quadratic factor (z−(−1+√3i))(z−(−1−√3i)) = z²+2z+4, compare coefficients in (z−c)(z²+2z+4)=z³+5z²+10z+12 to get c=−3. (ii) OR: factor 1+5w+10w²+12w³ = (3w+1)(4w²+2w+1)=0 and solve.

evidence.basis: (i) A1 for conjugate −1−√3i as root. EITHER: M1 sum of roots → (A1) (−1+√3i)+(−1−√3i)+c = −5 → (A1) c = −3. OR: M1 product of roots → (A1) 4c = −12 → (A1) c = −3. OR: (A1) quadratic factor z²+2z+4 → M1 coefficient comparison → (A1) −4c = −12. THEN A1: c = −3. (ii) METHOD 1: A2 for z = 1/w; A1, A1 for w = −1/3, (−1∓√3i)/4. METHOD 2: M1 factorisation; A1 for (3w+1)(4w²+2w+1)=0; A1, A1 for roots.

blocks.task_summary: Solve z² = 2z* (z ≠ 0) by expressing z = a+bi, find all roots.
method_path: Equate real and imaginary parts: a²−b² = 2a, 2ab = −2b
Case b=0: a²=2a → a=0 (reject, z≠0) or a=2 → z=2

evidence.basis: A1 for (a+bi)² = 2(a−bi); M1 expand and equate real/imaginary parts: a²−b²=2a, 2ab=−2b; M1 solve for a or b; A1 for b=0 → a=2 (real root z=2); A1 for a=−1 → b=±√3 (complex roots z=−1±√3i).

blocks.task_summary: Use substitution t = √x and integration by parts to show that ∫cos(√x)dx = 2√x sin(√x) + 2cos(√x) + C
method_path: Rewrite integral as ∫2t cos t dt
Integrate by parts: let u = 2t, dv = cos t dt, so du = 2dt, v = sin t
Obtain ∫2t cos t dt = 2t sin t − ∫2 sin t dt = 2t sin t + 2cos t + C
Back-substitute t = √x to obtain 2√x sin(√x) + 2cos(√x) + C

evidence.basis: Substitution t=√x (M1); dt/dx=1/(2√x) ⇒ dx=2t dt (A1); ∫cos(√x)dx=∫2t cos t dt (A1); attempts integration by parts (M1); u=2t, dv=cos t dt, du=2dt, v=sin t (A1); 2t sin t+2cos t+C (A1); substitution back yields result (AG)

blocks.task_summary: Write down expression for x_{n+1} given x_n = ((2n−1)²π²)/4
method_path: Replace n by n+1 in x_n = ((2n−1)²π²)/4

blocks.task_summary: Calculate area of region R_n = |∫_{x_n}^{x_{n+1}} cos(√x) dx|, giving answer as 4πn
method_path: Set up definite integral ∫_{x_n}^{x_{n+1}} cos(√x) dx with modulus for area
Evaluate sin and cos at odd multiples of π/2: cos terms vanish, sin terms give (−1)^n and (−1)^{n−1}

evidence.basis: area of R_n is |∫_{x_n}^{x_{n+1}} cos(√x)dx| (M1); antiderivative [2√x sin(√x)+2cos(√x)] (A1); substitute limits (M1); simplify using sin/cos at multiples of π/2 (A1,A1,A1); final result 4πn (A1)

blocks.task_summary: Show that the areas R_n = 4πn form an arithmetic sequence
method_path: Find common difference d = R_{n+1} − R_n = 4π(n+1) − 4πn
Conclude that constant common difference implies arithmetic sequence
accepted_alternatives: Compare R_n = 4πn to general arithmetic form u_n = dn + c, identify d = 4π and c = 0

evidence.basis: EITHER: d=R_{n+1}−R_n=4π(n+1)−4πn=4π constant (M1)(A1), so arithmetic (R1); OR: compare R_n=4πn to u_n=dn+c, d=4π, c=0 (M1)(M1)(A1)
